syllabus.clause: comparing old vs new pipeline outputs on identical input
full join-diff vs checksum bisection across systems (hash key ranges, recurse into mismatching segments)
and the cost of diffing TB-scale tables

items.item: a same-database diff uses an outer-join to diff the rows as efficiently and accurately as possible
a cross-database diff employs a divide and conquer algorithm based on hashing, optimized for few changes
data-diff splits the table into smaller segments, then checksums each segment in both databases, recursing into mismatching segments until it reaches the differing rows
this approach has performance within an order of magnitude of count(*) when there are few or no changes
real and double precision are inexact, variable-precision numeric types, and comparing two floating-point values for equality might not always work as expected
timestamp precision accepts an optional value from 0 to 6 fractional digits in the seconds field

sources.source: This topic's own real diff experiments

items.item: a full join-diff and a checksum-bisection diff, run against the same old/new fct_orders with a single planted column regression, find exactly the same mismatches while scanning very different numbers of rows
a tolerance band lets a harmless float-summation-order difference pass while still catching a real planted regression on the same comparison
a column-level summary built from the planted bug names the one changed column, how many rows it touched, and the size of the move
holding the number of real changes fixed while growing the table shows join-diff's cost scaling exactly with table size while bisection's relative advantage widens

The hook's real lesson is that a diff's own report format is itself a design choice with consequences -- a technically correct row count can be a worse deliverable than a slightly less complete but reviewable column summary.

A reader might assume checksum bisection trades correctness for speed -- it doesn't: a matching checksum is just as exact a proof of no-change as reading every row would be, assuming no hash collision, which is why this is a real optimization and not an approximation.

The choice between join-diff and bisection isn't really about table size alone -- it's about table size relative to the expected number of real changes; a table with almost every row changed gains little from bisection, since nearly every segment ends up mismatching anyway.

A tolerance band is itself a claim that needs its own justification, the same way the time-flakiness fix in the prior topic did -- too wide a band hides a real regression that happens to be small, too narrow a band flags harmless noise forever.

A column-level summary's real value isn't compression of the report -- it's that it turns an un-actionable fact ('something changed') into an actionable one ('this column, by this much'), which is what actually lets a human decide whether the change was intended.

This topic's cost curve holds the absolute number of real changes fixed on purpose, not the rate -- a fixed rate would make the number of changes grow with the table too, which would hide bisection's actual advantage rather than reveal it.

Running this technique on a plain schema copy instead of a true zero-copy clone or branch is a real simplification, not a cosmetic one -- a schema copy can drift from production between when it's taken and when the diff runs, a gap a true zero-copy branch closes.

The cost curve's real-world unit isn't rows scanned at all -- it's bytes read and compute-seconds billed, which this topic's own run approximates with a row count because a real warehouse's exact byte/dollar cost model is sourced differently per vendor.

Two checksum implementations that hash different column serializations of the same logical row would disagree even when the data is identical -- the checksum's own definition has to be fixed and shared between the old and new side, or the whole technique produces false positives.

This topic's join-diff and bisection diff are deliberately the same baseline the chapter-lab scorecard (topic 17) measures against -- the specific planted bug and table shape chosen here are the fixed, known case that scorecard will later ask how selectively it gets run.
